title: Arithmetic definability: enumerable sets and quantifiers
summary: An enumerable set is exactly a set described in arithmetic by an unbounded search followed by a bounded check.
abstract: A program may accept an input only after a long search; what arithmetic description captures exactly the inputs on which that search succeeds? In the standard natural numbers, the computably enumerable sets—those whose members a program can eventually recognize—are exactly the sets whose membership can be expressed by the existence of numerical witnesses followed by a bounded arithmetic check. Every quantifier in that check ranges over an explicitly bounded finite set. Universal descriptions obtained by negation capture exactly the sets whose nonmembers can be recognized, and having both kinds of description is equivalent to decidability. The halting set therefore has an arithmetic definition without a decision procedure. Requiring a program to halt on every input gives a further quantifier pattern: each input must have its own successful computation record. This separates a finite witness for one run from a requirement covering every possible input.
